interviewQuestions.question: Can you explain the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, with examples?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it around what I'd have to manage myself at each layer, then anchor each with a real product, since the abstraction ladder is really about where the line of managed responsibility sits.

With **IaaS** I get raw virtual machines, storage, and networking — an EC2 instance or a Compute Engine VM — and I'm responsible for the OS, patching, runtime installation, and scaling logic myself; the provider only guarantees the hardware and hypervisor layer beneath me. With **PaaS**, the platform manages the OS and runtime for me — I push code to something like Elastic Beanstalk, Heroku, or Cloud Run, and it handles provisioning, scaling, and load balancing without me ever touching a server; I still own my application code and its behavior. With **SaaS**, I don't manage any infrastructure or even application code — I just use a finished product like Gmail or Salesforce, and my only responsibility is configuration and the data I put into it.

The trade-off runs in a straight line: less operational control but more velocity as you move from IaaS toward SaaS. IaaS gives me the freedom to run anything, at the cost of running everything myself; SaaS gives me zero setup time, at the cost of accepting the vendor's feature set exactly as built.

In practice, most real companies use all three simultaneously for different systems — EC2 for a custom workload that needs specific tuning, a PaaS for an internal tool where velocity matters more than control, and SaaS like Salesforce for CRM where building it themselves would be pure waste. Picking one model for the whole org is usually a sign of not having thought about the trade-off per system.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as a spectrum of managed responsibility, not three unrelated buzzwords, and can ground each layer in a real, concrete product.

interviewQuestions.question: Where does FaaS (serverless functions) fit on the IaaS/PaaS/SaaS spectrum, and why is that placement genuinely debatable?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
FaaS sits at the far managed end of PaaS, and the placement is debatable because it removes even more than a typical PaaS does, to the point where some people argue it deserves its own category. A conventional PaaS still has you thinking about a running application process — it's up continuously, handling requests, and you configure autoscaling for it. FaaS removes the concept of a continuously running process entirely: you deploy a single function, the platform invokes it per event, and there's nothing running (and nothing costing money) between invocations.

The reason it's still usually placed under PaaS rather than getting its own tier: you're still managing application-level code and logic, same as PaaS, just at finer granularity — a single function instead of a whole app. That's a genuinely different unit of deployment, but it's not a different *kind* of responsibility split; the provider still owns the OS, runtime, and now also the entire execution lifecycle including scaling to zero.

Where the debate gets real: FaaS's execution model — cold starts, per-invocation billing, execution time limits — is different enough from a typical PaaS's always-on process model that some frameworks and vendors present serverless as its own fourth category alongside IaaS/PaaS/SaaS rather than a subset of PaaS. I'd mention this nuance in an interview rather than pretend the categorization is settled — it signals you've thought about the boundary instead of just memorizing a diagram.

**Testing:** whether you can place FaaS with reasoning instead of guessing, and acknowledge where the taxonomy itself is fuzzy.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Where FaaS actually fits

interviewQuestions.question: What is the shared responsibility model, and where does it actually shift as you move from IaaS to SaaS?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The shared responsibility model draws a line between what the cloud provider secures and what the customer secures, and that line moves predictably as you move up the abstraction ladder — the provider's share grows, the customer's share shrinks, but it never fully disappears.

On **IaaS**, the provider secures the physical data center, hardware, and hypervisor — "security of the cloud" — while the customer is responsible for the OS, patching, network configuration, and application-level security — "security in the cloud." A misconfigured security group or an unpatched OS on an EC2 instance is squarely the customer's problem; AWS securing that specific instance is not part of the deal.

On **PaaS**, the provider absorbs OS and runtime patching, so that specific risk moves to their side of the line — but the customer is still responsible for application-level vulnerabilities (an injection flaw in code they wrote), access control on who can deploy, and the data itself.

On **SaaS**, the provider secures nearly everything about the application, but the customer is still responsible for their own configuration and user access — who has admin rights in Salesforce, what data gets shared externally, whether MFA is enforced for their org's users. A SaaS breach caused by a customer leaving an admin account with a weak password is the customer's failure, not the vendor's, even though the vendor secured the application itself.

The point I'd make explicitly: "the cloud provider secures it" is never a complete sentence at any layer — there's always a customer-side responsibility that doesn't vanish just because the infrastructure below it is managed.

**Testing:** whether you know the line moves gradually rather than treating any layer as "fully secured by the vendor."
